# The Path

*Dhp 273-289, the Maggavagga — set 2, The Basic Diagnosis and the Path*

<p class="reading-meta"><strong>Reading time:</strong> about 3 min · 461 words</p>

[Skip to the translation](#translation){ .reader-skip-link }

## Before you read

This is the Path chapter of the Dhammapada: seventeen short verses about the
way out of dissatisfaction.

It opens by ranking things. The best path is the eightfold path, and there is
no other. Then comes the line many people remember from this chapter: *you
yourselves must make the effort; Tathāgatas only tell the way.*

Verses 277 to 279 are the heart of it. Each takes one of three facts, that
everything put together is impermanent, that it is unsatisfactory, and that
all phenomena are not-self, and says the same thing about it: when you see
this with discernment, you grow disenchanted, and that is the path. AN 3.136
states the same three facts in prose.

The rest is practical: get up when it is time to get up, guard your speech,
cut down the forest of desire, and do not assume there will always be more
time.

The numbers beside the verses are the Dhammapada's own verse numbers.

## Translation

### Verses

<span class="verse-number">273</span><span class="verse-line">Of paths, the eightfold is the best;</span>
<span class="verse-line">of truths, the four statements;</span>
<span class="verse-line">of dhammas, fading is the best;</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">and of those who walk on two feet, the one with vision.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">274</span><span class="verse-line">This is the path; there is no other</span>
<span class="verse-line">for the purifying of vision.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Follow this path:</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">it leaves Māra bewildered.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">275</span><span class="verse-line">Following it,</span>
<span class="verse-line">you will make an end of dissatisfaction.</span>
<span class="verse-line">I have taught you the path,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">knowing how the arrow is drawn out.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">276</span><span class="verse-line">You yourselves must make the effort;</span>
<span class="verse-line">Tathāgatas only tell the way.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Those who follow it and practice the mental themes</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">will be freed from Māra's bonds.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">277</span><span class="verse-line">'All that has been put together is impermanent':</span>
<span class="verse-line">when someone sees this with discernment,</span>
<span class="verse-line">they grow disenchanted with dissatisfaction.</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">This is the path to purity.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">278</span><span class="verse-line">'All that has been put together is unsatisfactory':</span>
<span class="verse-line">when someone sees this with discernment,</span>
<span class="verse-line">they grow disenchanted with dissatisfaction.</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">This is the path to purity.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">279</span><span class="verse-line">'All phenomena are not-self':</span>
<span class="verse-line">when someone sees this with discernment,</span>
<span class="verse-line">they grow disenchanted with dissatisfaction.</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">This is the path to purity.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">280</span><span class="verse-line">Not getting up when it is time to get up,</span>
<span class="verse-line">young and strong, but given to idleness,</span>
<span class="verse-line">their attitude and mind sunk low, the lazy</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">do not find the path by discernment.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">281</span><span class="verse-line">Guarding speech, well restrained in mind,</span>
<span class="verse-line">doing nothing unwholesome with the body:</span>
<span class="verse-line">keep these three paths of action clean,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">and you will win the path the seers made known.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">282</span><span class="verse-line">From practice, wisdom grows;</span>
<span class="verse-line">without practice, wisdom wastes away.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Knowing this two-way road</span>
<span class="verse-line">to growth and to decline,</span>
<span class="verse-line">set yourself on the way</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">by which wisdom grows.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">283</span><span class="verse-line">Cut down the forest, not just a tree:</span>
<span class="verse-line">danger is born from the forest.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Once you have cut down the forest and the undergrowth,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">be free of the forest, bhikkhus.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">284</span><span class="verse-line">As long as the undergrowth of a man's desire for women</span>
<span class="verse-line">is not cut down, even the smallest bit of it,</span>
<span class="verse-line">so long his mind stays bound,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">like a suckling calf to its mother.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">285</span><span class="verse-line">Cut out your fondness for yourself,</span>
<span class="verse-line">as you would pull an autumn lily with your hand.</span>
<span class="verse-line">Develop only the path to peace,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">the nibbāna the Sugata taught.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">286</span><span class="verse-line">'Here I will spend the rains,</span>
<span class="verse-line">here the winter and the summer':</span>
<span class="verse-line">so the fool thinks,</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">and does not see what may cut it short.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">287</span><span class="verse-line">That man, intoxicated with children and cattle,</span>
<span class="verse-line">his mind attached,</span>
<span class="verse-line">death seizes and carries off</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">as a great flood a sleeping village.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">288</span><span class="verse-line">Children are no shelter,</span>
<span class="verse-line">nor a father, nor relatives.</span>
<span class="verse-line">For someone overtaken by the Ender</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">there is no shelter among kin.</span>
{: .verse }

<span class="verse-number">289</span><span class="verse-line">Seeing the force of this,</span>
<span class="verse-line">the wise, restrained by conduct,</span>
<span class="verse-line">should quickly clear the path</span>
<span class="verse-line verse-line--last">that leads to nibbāna.</span>
{: .verse }

The twentieth chapter, on the path, is finished.

<summary>Words used in this translation (12)</summary>
<dl>
<dt><dfn>arrow</dfn></dt>
<dd>A recurring image across these texts with more than one meaning. In MN 63 it&#x27;s a poisoned arrow -- refusing treatment until every background fact about the wound is known first, a warning against blocking practice with unanswerable questions. In SN 36.6 it&#x27;s a different image entirely: an ordinary person&#x27;s pain is one arrow, and the extra suffering added on top of it is a second, avoidable arrow.</dd>
<dt><dfn>bhikkhus</dfn></dt>
<dd>Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha&#x27;s usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly &quot;friends&quot; in force.</dd>
<dt><dfn>body</dfn></dt>
<dd>The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.</dd>
<dt><dfn>conduct</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;sīla&quot; (often translated &quot;morality&quot; or &quot;virtue&quot;) -- how a person actually behaves, taken as the ground the rest of the practice grows on rather than as a set of rules to obey.</dd>
<dt><dfn>dissatisfaction</dfn></dt>
<dd>This translation&#x27;s rendering of &quot;dukkha,&quot; the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated &quot;suffering,&quot; but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.</dd>
<dt><dfn>fading</dfn></dt>
<dd>The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.</dd>
<dt><dfn>flood</dfn></dt>
<dd>A force that overwhelms and carries a person along unless it is crossed. SN 1.1 leaves the image open rather than defining it as one specific mental state.</dd>
<dt><dfn>knowing</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;viññāṇa&quot; (often translated &quot;consciousness&quot;) -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.</dd>
<dt><dfn>nibbāna</dfn></dt>
<dd>The end of greed, hatred, and confusion -- the traditional goal of Buddhist practice. Left untranslated because no single English word covers it; &quot;quenching&quot; is the closest one-word gloss.</dd>
<dt><dfn>not-self</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;anattā&quot; -- not a claim that you don&#x27;t exist, but that nothing in experience holds up as a fixed, ownable &quot;self&quot; when actually examined.</dd>
<dt><dfn>put together</dfn></dt>
<dd>In &quot;all that has been put together&quot;, this project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;saṅkhārā&quot; on its result side: anything assembled from conditions, as opposed to the activity of assembling.</dd>
<dt><dfn>unwholesome</dfn></dt>
<dd>This project&#x27;s rendering of &quot;akusala&quot; -- roughly, mentally and ethically harmful: blameworthy, leads to harm, and is criticized by people with good judgment.</dd>
</dl>

*[arrow]: A recurring image across these texts with more than one meaning. In MN 63 it's a poisoned arrow -- refusing treatment until every background fact about the wound is known first, a warning against blocking practice with unanswerable questions. In SN 36.6 it's a different image entirely: an ordinary person's pain is one arrow, and the extra suffering added on top of it is a second, avoidable arrow.
*[bhikkhus]: Buddhist monks -- those who have left household life to practise full time. The Buddha's usual way of addressing the assembly, roughly "friends" in force.
*[body]: The physical body, as distinct from speech and the mental side of experience.
*[conduct]: This project's rendering of "sīla" (often translated "morality" or "virtue") -- how a person actually behaves, taken as the ground the rest of the practice grows on rather than as a set of rules to obey.
*[dissatisfaction]: This translation's rendering of "dukkha," the Buddhist term for the unsatisfying, unstable quality of ordinary experience. Often translated "suffering," but that can sound more dramatic than the everyday sense of things not quite being right.
*[fading]: The fading away of attraction and investment in experience, as passion cools.
*[flood]: A force that overwhelms and carries a person along unless it is crossed. SN 1.1 leaves the image open rather than defining it as one specific mental state.
*[knowing]: This project's rendering of "viññāṇa" (often translated "consciousness") -- bare awareness of an object through one of the senses or the mind.
*[nibbāna]: The end of greed, hatred, and confusion -- the traditional goal of Buddhist practice. Left untranslated because no single English word covers it; "quenching" is the closest one-word gloss.
*[not-self]: This project's rendering of "anattā" -- not a claim that you don't exist, but that nothing in experience holds up as a fixed, ownable "self" when actually examined.
*[put together]: In "all that has been put together", this project's rendering of "saṅkhārā" on its result side: anything assembled from conditions, as opposed to the activity of assembling.
*[unwholesome]: This project's rendering of "akusala" -- roughly, mentally and ethically harmful: blameworthy, leads to harm, and is criticized by people with good judgment.
